section.title: Teaching Sound Doctrine
section.sectionRationale: Over against the false teachers, Titus is to teach what accords with sound doctrine. Paul works household by household, older men and women, young women and men, and slaves, showing what godliness looks like in each, then grounds the whole ethic in the great gospel statement of the grace of God that has appeared and will appear again. Instruction and gospel form one movement.
section.thesis: Sound doctrine produces beautiful lives across every station, and the engine of that transformation is the grace of God that has appeared in Christ to save and to train us, as we await the glorious appearing of our great God and Savior.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the household instructions that adorn the teaching about God our Savior; then the theological heart, the grace of God that has appeared, redeeming a people zealous for good deeds, with a closing charge to Titus to speak with authority.

units.label: Sound doctrine in the household
units.note: godliness for every age and station

verses.text: But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with {{hygiaino|sound}} doctrine.
Older men are to be temperate, dignified, {{sophron|self-controlled}}, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance.
Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good.
In this way they can train the young women to love their husbands and children,
to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited.
In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled.
In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity,
and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us.
Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative,
not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our {{soter|Savior}}.

units.label: The grace of God has appeared
units.note: the gospel that trains and redeems

verses.text: For the {{charis|grace}} of God has {{epiphaneia|appeared}}, bringing salvation to everyone.
It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age,
as we await the blessed hope and glorious {{epiphaneia|appearance}} of our {{megasTheos|great God and Savior}} Jesus Christ.
He gave Himself for us to {{lutroo|redeem}} us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.
Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.

hygiaino.gloss: To be healthy or sound, the root of hygiene. Applied to doctrine, it means teaching that is spiritually wholesome and life-giving, the opposite of the diseased talk of the false teachers. Sound doctrine in Titus is never abstract: it produces the healthy, godly lives described in this very chapter.

sophron.gloss: Self-controlled, sensible, of a sound mind. The word and its cognates saturate this chapter, urged on older men, young women, and young men, and named as the very thing grace trains us toward in verse 12. It is the mark of a people no longer ruled by worldly passions but governed by God's grace.

soter.gloss: Saviour, one who rescues. A key title in Titus, applied to both God the Father and Christ Jesus. Here even the humble faithfulness of slaves is said to adorn the teaching about God our Saviour, showing that the gospel's beauty is displayed in ordinary, honest lives.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's undeserved favour and saving kindness. In verse 11 grace is almost personified: it has appeared in the person and work of Christ, bringing salvation and actively training God's people. Grace is not only the ground of pardon but the power that reshapes how we live.

epiphaneia.gloss: An appearing or manifestation, used of a royal or divine arrival. Titus 2 speaks of two such appearings: grace has already appeared in Christ's first coming, verse 11, and we await His glorious appearing at the second, verse 13. Christian life is lived between these two shining moments.

megasTheos.gloss: Our great God and Savior. By a well-known feature of Greek grammar, the single phrase most naturally refers to one person, Jesus Christ, making this one of the clearest New Testament statements of Christ's full deity. The one we await is our great God and our Saviour in one.

lutroo.gloss: To redeem, to ransom by paying a price to set free. It recalls Israel's redemption from Egypt and the price of a slave's release. Christ gave Himself as the ransom to free us from all lawlessness and to make us His own purified people, so redemption leads straight to a transformed, good-works life.

basic.context: In contrast to the false teachers, Titus is to teach truth that produces good lives. Paul goes group by group, older men and women, younger women and men, and slaves, describing the godly character each should show. Then he explains the power behind it all: the grace of God that appeared in Jesus to save us, train us, and make us His own people, eager to do good.
basic.hermeneutics: The instructions to different groups reflect the household structures of the first century, and the underlying call, to godliness, self-control, and integrity that make the gospel attractive, holds for every age. The section on slaves describes how to live faithfully within an existing system; it is not an endorsement of slavery. The gospel statement in verses 11-14 is the key that unlocks the whole passage.
basic.originalLanguages: Titus is to speak what accords with hygiaino, sound or healthy, doctrine. Self-control, sophron, runs through the chapter. Everything aims to adorn the teaching about God our soter, our Saviour. The heart is the charis, grace, that has appeared, epiphaneia, in Christ, our great God and Saviour, who gave Himself to redeem, lutroo, a people for Himself.
basic.typology: Christ giving Himself to redeem a people for His own possession echoes the exodus, when God ransomed Israel to be His treasured possession. Jesus is the greater Redeemer, and the church is the true treasured people, purified by His blood.
basic.christ: This is one of the clearest gospel summaries in the New Testament. The grace of God has appeared in Jesus at His first coming; He gave Himself to redeem us and purify a people zealous for good works; and we now wait for His glorious second appearing. Verse 13 calls Him our great God and Saviour, a plain statement of His full deity.
basic.god: God is our Saviour whose grace has appeared to everyone. His grace does not merely forgive; it teaches and trains us to say no to ungodliness and to live upright lives. He is a God who redeems a people to belong to Him and to be eager for good.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 2 shows salvation by grace leading to good works God prepared. First Peter 2 calls the church a people for God's own possession. And Exodus 19 names Israel God's treasured possession, the pattern fulfilled in Christ's redeemed people.
basic.oneStory: The gospel here spans the whole story: grace appearing in Christ's first coming, a people redeemed and purified as God's own possession like Israel of old, and the sure hope of His glorious return. We live in the middle, between the two appearings, being trained by grace to live godly lives that make the gospel beautiful.

context.literary:
The chapter opens with a sharp turn. Chapter 1 ended on false teachers whose deeds deny what they claim, and verse 1 begins with a pointed but as for you. Titus is told to speak what fits sound doctrine, and the rest of the chapter shows what fitting looks like. The section has the shape of a sandwich. Verses 1 and 15 frame it with charges to Titus himself, and between them lie two blocks: a series of instructions to groups in verses 2 to 10, and the great gospel statement of verses 11 to 14, opened with the little word for, which makes grace the ground of everything that came before.

The first block goes in order: older men, older women, younger women, younger men, Titus himself, and slaves. Two of the groups, the older women and Titus, are described through the teaching they pass on to others, which builds a chain: Titus teaches, older women train younger women, and the whole community learns. The instructions are bound together by three purpose clauses that explain why behaviour matters: so that the word of God will not be discredited, verse 5; so that opponents will be ashamed with nothing bad to say, verse 8; and so that slaves will adorn the teaching about God our Savior, verse 10. Each looks outward, at how outsiders will judge the gospel.

The gospel block, verses 11 to 14, is built around two appearings, the first of grace in verse 11 and the second of glory in verse 13, with the saving work of Christ in verse 14 between them. The same Greek family of words occurs in 3:4, so the two chapters answer each other. Verse 15 then returns to Titus with three verbs, speak, encourage and rebuke, and a command about authority.
context.historical:
The household was the basic unit of Greco-Roman society. It included the husband, wife, children, slaves, freedmen and often dependants, and its good order was a matter of public concern. Writers of the period regularly commented on how households should be run, and a new religion that met in houses could be accused of upsetting them. Paul's counsel, like that of Peter in 1 Peter 2:11 to 3:7, shows believers living so that their neighbours have nothing to accuse them of.

Slavery was widespread across the Roman empire, and slaves made up a large share of the population. Many were skilled and educated, and some held positions of trust. Paul does not write a law against the institution here, but his wider teaching undermines it: he tells Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, Philemon 16, and he lists the slave trader among the lawless in 1 Timothy 1:10. In Titus the instruction is addressed to slaves who were part of the churches, and it frames their work as a chance to make the gospel attractive.

The words savior and appearing carried weight in the surrounding world. The title savior was given to gods and rulers who rescued cities and nations, and the word for appearing was used for the arrival of a ruler or the visible help of a god. By using both of Jesus, Paul places the gospel in direct contrast to the claims of power around the churches. On Crete the cults of the old gods and the cult of the emperor were part of daily life, so the claim that grace has appeared in Jesus, our great God and Savior, was bold.
context.canonical:
Titus 2 belongs to a series of household instructions in the New Testament: Ephesians 5:21 to 6:9, Colossians 3:18 to 4:1, and 1 Peter 2:18 to 3:7. They share a pattern of addressing particular groups, grounding duty in Christ, and attending to the witness of the church before the world. What makes Titus distinctive is the emphasis on teaching one another: the older women train the younger, and the whole is anchored in a compact gospel summary.

The passage looks back to the exodus language of redemption. The phrase a people for His own possession in verse 14 echoes the way God described Israel in Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6, and the promise that He will redeem them from all their iniquities in Psalm 130:8. It also recalls Ezekiel's promise of cleansing and zeal for the Lord. Peter applies the same language to the church in 1 Peter 2:9.

The passage looks forward to the day of Christ. The blessed hope of verse 13 joins the long line of texts about the day of the Lord, and the language of appearing, epiphaneia, is used by Paul for the return of Christ in 2 Thessalonians 2:8, 1 Timothy 6:14, and 2 Timothy 4:1 and 4:8. The line about the grace of God that has appeared is paired with 2 Timothy 1:10, which says grace has been revealed through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death. Titus 2:11-14 is among the most quoted summaries of the gospel in the church's history because it joins what Christ did, what grace does and what we wait for.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants Titus to understand that sound doctrine is not a set of statements kept in a drawer. In the Pastoral Letters it is a teaching that makes people healthy, which is the meaning behind the word. The test of the teaching is the life of the people who receive it. After the false teachers of chapter 1, who deny God by their works, Paul states the alternative in verse 1 and then spends nine verses describing ordinary Christian living in homes and workplaces.

He has three purposes in view. The first is protection: if believers live well, no one will be able to say the word of God is a cover for disorder, verse 5, or find anything bad to say, verse 8. The second is attraction: the teaching is meant to be adorned, made beautiful, by the way slaves work and all believers live, verse 10. The third is motive. Paul does not simply ask for better behaviour, he roots it in grace. The same grace that brings salvation trains, verse 12, and the Savior who redeemed us made a people zealous for good deeds, verse 14.

The first hearers, the Cretan believers, had a reputation to overcome. They were to see that the cure for the culture's vices is not a stricter code but a transformed people, formed by grace and waiting for Christ.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage mixes descriptions of a first century household with commands that reach every age. What carries over without any question is the character: temperance, dignity, love, endurance, purity, kindness, integrity and good works, along with the commitment to teach, train and set an example. These apply to older and younger, women and men in every culture.

The specific forms are more tied to their setting. The call for wives to be submissive and managers of their households, and for slaves to submit, is addressed to believers in a time when these structures were part of the world. The text describes how to live faithfully within them without endorsing slavery as an institution, as the wider New Testament shows. Christians apply the household instructions by asking what the underlying principle is, so that the word of God will not be discredited, and by weighing carefully where the apostle is describing a way to live in a given world and where he is stating a lasting order. The gospel summary of verses 11 to 14 is not bound to any culture at all and is the standard by which every application is tested.

debates.question: How should the call for wives to be submissive to their own husbands be understood?

views.label: A lasting pattern of wifely submission
views.case: Complementarian readers see the instruction as part of a continuing order in marriage, in line with Ephesians 5:22-24 and 1 Peter 3:1-6, where headship and submission reflect Christ and the church. They note that the Greek verb is used of the church's relation to Christ and that Paul gives a reason tied to the word of God, not just to custom.

views.label: A witness strategy for a particular setting
views.case: Egalitarian readers stress the stated purpose, that the word of God not be discredited, and argue that the instruction applies the principle of mutual submission, Ephesians 5:21, to a context where women's perceived disorder would give opponents a charge. They say the command expresses cultural wisdom more than a fixed order.

debates.bearing: Both agree that the verse is aimed at honouring the gospel and that submission is never a mandate for mistreatment, since the verb is voluntary arranging oneself under another. Where the two differ is whether the pattern is permanent or situational. The wise reading looks to the whole of the New Testament on marriage and holds the passage with humility.

debates.question: Does grace bringing salvation to all people teach that everyone is saved?

views.label: Grace for all kinds of people
views.case: The verse follows a list of classes of people: old and young, men and women, slaves. On this reading Paul means the gospel is not limited to one group, since the saving grace has appeared to people from every rank, and the following verses speak of a particular people redeemed.

views.label: Grace offered to every human being
views.case: Others take the phrase as a statement of the universal scope of the offer. They note that Paul says elsewhere that God wants all people to be saved, 1 Timothy 2:4, and is the Savior of all, especially of those who believe, 1 Timothy 4:10, and that Jesus is the one mediator for all, 1 Timothy 2:5-6.

views.label: Universal salvation
views.case: A few say the verse teaches that grace actually saves every person in the end. This reading does not fit the immediate context, where grace trains a people who renounce ungodliness, nor the warnings elsewhere in the letter, such as 1:16 and 3:10-11.

debates.bearing: All the major readings agree that grace has appeared on a scale wide enough to reach every kind of person, and that it saves through Christ. The text does not say every person is saved, and the next verses focus on those who are redeemed and purified.

debates.question: Is the great God and Savior in verse 13 one person or two?

views.label: One person, Jesus Christ
views.case: A single article governs both nouns, God and Savior, and the title is followed by Jesus Christ, so the natural reading is that Jesus is both our great God and Savior. The title Savior is used of Jesus in 1:4, 3:6, and the parallel in 2 Peter 1:1 has the same form. Verse 14 goes on to describe what He did, not what the Father did.

views.label: Two persons, the Father and Jesus
views.case: Others hold that Paul speaks of the glory of the great God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, so that God means the Father. They point out that the Father is called God and Savior in 1:3, 2:10 and 3:4, and argue that Paul more often distinguishes the Father as God from the Son as Lord.

debates.bearing: The grammar and the flow of the thought, the appearing of the glory of a person who gave Himself for us, favour the first reading, which is also how most early church writers took it. If correct, this is one of the plainest places where the New Testament calls Jesus God.

study.originalLanguages:
The verbs in this chapter trace the way grace works. In verse 12 grace is said to instruct us, from the verb paideuo, which comes from the word for a child and covers teaching, training and discipline. It is the verb Hebrews uses for a father's discipline, Hebrews 12:6-11. Grace here is not only a pardon but a tutor who takes a person in hand. What it teaches is, first, to renounce, arneomai, ungodliness and worldly passions. The same verb is used of the false teachers in 1:16, who deny God by their deeds. Grace trains believers to deny the very things the false teachers affirm in practice, and to affirm in practice what those teachers deny.

The three adverbs of verse 12, sensibly, righteously and godly, describe three directions: toward oneself, toward others and toward God. Self-control, the word sophron family that runs through the chapter, covers the first, a settled and sound mind. The phrase in the present age sets the Christian's life between two ages, the one that is passing and the one coming, in the same way as Galatians 1:4.

The words epiphaino and epiphaneia, appear and appearance, both come from a root meaning to shine upon, and the first of them describes grace as having dawned like light. The verb in verse 11 is in the aorist, a completed event, while the noun in verse 13 points to a future event. Paul uses the same noun for the return of Christ in other letters, 2 Thessalonians 2:8, 1 Timothy 6:14 and 2 Timothy 4:1. Between them he places the middle verb, He gave Himself.

The word for adorn in verse 10, kosmeo, gives us cosmetics and cosmos, and means to arrange beautifully. It is the word for a bride adorned for her husband in Revelation 21:2 and for a woman's inner beauty in 1 Peter 3:3-5. Slaves are not asked merely to behave but to make the gospel lovely.

The word translated steal in verse 10, nosphizo, means to set aside for oneself, to pilfer, and it is the verb used when Ananias and Sapphira kept back part of the price in Acts 5:2-3. And the phrase a people for His own possession, laos periousios, is the wording of the Greek Old Testament in Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6 and 14:2, so Paul takes language for Israel and gives it to the church. Redeem, lutroo, in verse 14 is also used in a line that echoes Psalm 130:8, that God will redeem His people from all their iniquities.

typology.type: The redeemed people of the exodus, verse 14
typology.fulfillment: God freed Israel from Egypt to be His own people, His treasured possession among all the peoples, Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6. They were bought out of slavery by His mighty hand, Exodus 6:6, and set apart to serve Him. Paul takes the same description and applies it to a people redeemed by Christ, who gave Himself, not by the blood of lambs but by His own life, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The escalation is from a nation delivered from a human tyrant to a people drawn from every nation and freed from all lawlessness. The type falls short because Israel needed redemption again and again, while Christ's single offering is enough.

typology.type: The slave who adorns his master's teaching, verses 9-10
typology.fulfillment: The picture of the faithful servant runs from Joseph in Potiphar's house, Genesis 39:2-6, to the servant of the Lord in Isaiah 42 and 52:13 to 53:12. Paul asks slaves to bring credit to the gospel by faithful service. Jesus is the true servant: He took the form of a slave and became obedient, Philippians 2:7-8, and said He came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45. The correspondence is real as a pattern of conduct. It breaks in that the servant of the Lord does not just adorn the message, He is the message.

typology.type: Two appearings of grace and glory
typology.fulfillment: Israel's story was shaped by appearances of God, from Sinai to the temple, each pointing to a fuller coming. Paul's two appearings are the climax: the grace of God that has appeared in the life, death and resurrection of Jesus, and the glory that will appear when He returns. Hebrews gives the same shape, that He appeared once to put away sin by sacrifice and will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to bring salvation, Hebrews 9:26-28. The Old Testament pattern of promise and fulfilment is now doubled: the first appearing is accomplished and the second is certain. The type is incomplete until the second appearing.

typology.type: The household order and Christ with His church
typology.fulfillment: Paul grounds marriage in a larger picture. The relation of husband and wife is a great mystery, he says, that speaks of Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32, and the Old Testament prophets portray God as the husband of His people, Hosea 2:19-20 and Isaiah 54:5. Titus applies the picture in the opposite direction, so that love, purity and kindness in the home display what Christ's love is like. The household is the stage on which the gospel is seen. Yet the type is limited: no earthly marriage can perfectly reflect Christ's self-giving love, and every marriage depends on His grace.

study.christ:
This chapter does not just lead to Christ, it names Him in three of the most compact statements about Him in the New Testament. Verse 10 calls God our Savior, and verse 13 calls Jesus Christ our great God and Savior, so the title the Greek world gave to emperors is given to a crucified Jew from Nazareth. Titus 1:3-4 and 3:4-6 apply the same title to the Father and to the Son. The Father saves, and the Son saves, and the two are not rivals. Paul does not argue for the deity of Christ, he simply assumes it and builds a hope upon it.

The chapter presents Him as an event in history. The grace of God has appeared, verse 11, and the single verb sums up His coming, life, death and resurrection. It names a particular time when the saving kindness of God became visible. The second appearing is future, verse 13, and Paul calls it the blessed hope, so the whole of Christian existence is stretched between the two.

Verse 14 describes what He did with a sentence that could be a creed: He gave Himself for us. The offering was personal, not a payment taken from a purse but His own life, and the beneficiaries are the people who are named with us. Two things happen through it. He redeems us from all lawlessness, the language of ransom that Jesus used about Himself in Mark 10:45, and He purifies for Himself a people, the language of cleansing that Ezekiel 37:23 promises. The result is a people zealous for good deeds, so good works are the fruit and not the price.

The chapter also displays Christ as the pattern. Slaves who adorn the teaching about God our Savior are following the one who took the form of a slave, Philippians 2:7. Titus is to be an example by good works, verse 7, as Jesus left an example, 1 Peter 2:21. The grace that trains us is the grace of a person who has gone ahead.

Guard against forced links. The groups in the household are not hidden portraits of Christ. But the way grace is placed in the middle is no accident. Everything asked of the old, the young, the free and the enslaved flows from what He has done and who He is. The hope of His appearing is the motive that makes patient, sensible living possible, for those who wait for Him are those whose lives are being turned toward Him.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who is for people and who is concerned with how they live. He is first of all Savior, a title used here three times for the Father and the Son together, and it means He actively rescues. The passage presents salvation not as His reaction to human effort but as an initiative: the grace of God has appeared, and it brings salvation to people. This is a God who comes to meet people, not one who waits for them to climb.

He is a God whose grace has a purpose. The same grace that forgives also trains, and the training is not harsh but is like a patient tutor teaching a child. A common mistake is to treat grace as permission, but Paul presents it as power: it empowers a person to say no to ungodliness and yes to a self-controlled, righteous and godly life. This shows God's character as holy and generous together. He does not lower His standard to pardon us, and He does not demand a standard without giving the grace to meet it.

He is a God who cares about ordinary life. The chapter spends more time on the way old men talk and young women work than on any abstract doctrine. A God who is concerned with the temper of an old man and the honesty of a slave is a God who takes seriously the places where most people spend their lives. He is not found only in worship services but in kitchens and workplaces.

He is a God who cares about His reputation among outsiders, and He ties that reputation to His people. The word of God may be discredited, His teaching may be adorned, and opponents may be put to shame. This is not vanity. It shows that He has chosen to make Himself known through a people, so the way they live bears witness to who He is.

He is also a God who owns a people. He redeemed us to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, so His love is a covenant love. We are not merely forgiven individuals, we are His. For worship, the chapter calls us to awe at the God who appeared, gratitude for the grace that trains, and eager waiting for the appearing of the great God and Savior, with a life that makes His teaching beautiful to those watching.

crossReferences.note: Another household passage, in which Paul grounds the duties of wives, husbands, children, slaves and masters in Christ and the church. It shows that the Titus 2 instructions are part of a wider apostolic pattern and that submission is set within mutual care, since the passage begins with submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.

Peter calls the church a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession. This applies to the church the language Titus 2:14 uses of the redeemed people, and it shows that the exodus titles of Israel now describe all who belong to Christ.

At Sinai God tells Israel that if they keep His covenant they will be His treasured possession among all peoples, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. This is the background for the phrase a people for His own possession in Titus 2:14, where Christ's redemption brings about what God promised His people.

The psalmist calls Israel to hope in the Lord because with Him is plentiful redemption, and He Himself will redeem Israel from all their iniquities. Titus 2:14 echoes this, with Christ giving Himself to redeem us from all lawlessness, so the psalm's hope finds its answer in the cross.

Paul says God saved us and called us, not by our works but by His own purpose and grace, now revealed through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death. It is a close parallel to Titus 2:11-14, stressing grace given before time and made visible by the appearing.

Paul answers the objection that grace invites sin by showing that those who have died with Christ cannot go on living in sin. This is the same logic as Titus 2:12, where grace trains us to renounce ungodliness, and both texts insist that free grace leads to changed lives, not careless ones.

Christ appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin by His sacrifice, and He will appear a second time to bring salvation to those who wait for Him. The two appearings of Titus 2:11 and 13 are laid out here, with the same movement from sacrifice to glory.

Peter addresses those who have received a faith through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ, using the same form of title as Titus 2:13. Two apostles, writing independently, call Jesus both God and Savior in one phrase, which strengthens the case for reading Titus 2:13 as a statement of His deity.

Christ, who was in the form of God, took the form of a slave, humbled Himself to death on a cross, and was exalted. It is the pattern behind Titus 2:9-10, because the slave who serves faithfully follows the one who became a servant, and the gospel gives dignity to humble work.

Paul tells Timothy to let no one look down on his youth but to be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. It parallels Titus 2:7 and 2:15, where Titus is to be an example and not to be despised, which shows that the leader's life must back up his teaching.

study.oneStory:
The gospel at the centre of Titus 2 belongs to the movement of the whole Bible, from a good creation to a broken one, to redemption and then a renewed creation. The grace that has appeared answers the problem that began in Genesis 3, where humanity was cut off from God's presence by distrust of His word. It also answers Israel's long history of failure, when God's people were repeatedly redeemed and repeatedly wandered. Paul claims that God has now acted decisively. The Savior has come, the ransom is paid, and a people is being purified.

The phrase a people for His own possession draws a straight line to Sinai. God rescued Israel from Egypt and set them apart as His treasured possession so that they would show the nations what He is like. Israel's story is the story of a people who bore that name and often failed it. Titus says that in Christ the same calling is fulfilled in a people from every background, purified from the inside and eager to do good. The household instructions are not an add-on but the way this people shows the nations what God is like, in homes, work and friendships that look different.

The chapter also stretches across time. The present age is a period of training under grace. It is lived in the middle of two appearings, and the church is neither in the old age nor yet in the new. The hope of the appearing of the great God and Savior is what gives the present its shape: sensible, upright, godly living while we wait.

The story ends where Paul's hope points, with the appearing of Christ and the arrival of the new creation. The marriage of the Lamb in Revelation 19 and 21 completes what the household metaphors only hint at, with the church adorned as a bride, Revelation 21:2. The same word, adorn, that describes a slave's faithful work in Titus 2:10 is used of the final beauty of the people He redeemed. What is done in the small, ordinary places of life in grace now is preparation for a world in which God dwells with His people and every tear is wiped away.

sermon.title: The Grace of God Appeared
sermon.why: In this Look at the Book study on Titus 2:11-14, Piper traces how the grace of God appeared in the person of Jesus, not a mere message, and how that grace both saves and trains us as we await the blessed hope. A clear, orthodox exposition of this movement's gospel heart.

quiz.q: What is the aim of the godly conduct Paul urges on each group?

options.text: That the word of God and the teaching about our Savior will be adorned, not discredited.
options.note: Verses 5 and 10 tie behaviour to the credibility and beauty of the gospel.

options.text: That believers will earn their salvation by good behaviour.
options.note: Good conduct flows from grace, verse 11; it does not earn salvation.

options.text: That Christians will win social status and comfort.
options.note: The goal is the gospel's honour, not personal advancement.

options.text: That the church will withdraw from the watching world.
options.note: The point is a witness before outsiders, not withdrawal.

quiz.q: According to verse 11, what has the grace of God done?

options.text: It has appeared in Christ, bringing salvation to everyone.
options.note: Grace has appeared, the gospel's first appearing, bringing salvation.

options.text: It has appeared only to a spiritual elite.
options.note: Grace has appeared for people of every station, not a secret few.

options.text: It has removed all need for godly living.
options.note: The very next verse says grace trains us to live godly lives.

options.text: It has not yet appeared and remains only future.
options.note: Grace has already appeared in Christ's first coming; we await the second.

quiz.q: What does grace train us to do while we wait for Christ?

options.text: To renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
options.note: Verse 12 makes grace an active teacher of holy living.

options.text: To do whatever we please, since we are forgiven.
options.note: That misreads grace; grace instructs us to renounce ungodliness.

options.text: To withdraw and simply wait passively.
options.note: We wait actively, living godly lives in the present age.

options.text: To trust in our own good works for acceptance.
options.note: Grace, not works, saves; it then reshapes how we live.

quiz.q: Who is described as our great God and Savior in verse 13?

options.text: Jesus Christ, named as both our great God and our Savior.
options.note: The grammar most naturally applies the whole phrase to Christ, affirming His deity.

options.text: Only God the Father, separate from Jesus.
options.note: A minority read it this way, but the phrase points to Christ Himself.

options.text: An angel sent to represent God.
options.note: The text speaks of God and Savior, not an angel.

options.text: Titus, as God's appointed leader.
options.note: The title belongs to Christ, whose appearing we await.

quiz.q: Why did Christ give Himself for us, according to verse 14?

options.text: To redeem us from all lawlessness and purify a people for His own, zealous for good deeds.
options.note: Redemption produces a purified people eager to do good, verse 14.

options.text: To leave us exactly as we were.
options.note: He redeems in order to purify and transform, not to leave us unchanged.

options.text: To reward those who first made themselves worthy.
options.note: He gave Himself for us; the initiative and price are His, not ours.

options.text: To free us so we can live however we like.
options.note: He frees us from lawlessness to make us zealous for good deeds.

quiz.q: How should Titus deliver this teaching, according to verse 15?

options.text: Speaking, encouraging, and rebuking with all authority, letting no one despise him.
options.note: Verse 15 charges Titus to teach boldly and with authority.

options.text: Timidly, so as not to upset anyone.
options.note: He is to encourage and rebuke with authority, not shrink back.

options.text: Only in private, never openly.
options.note: He is to speak these things openly and with authority.

options.text: As his personal opinion, carrying no weight.
options.note: He speaks with all authority as Christ's minister.

questions: Paul ties everyday conduct to whether the gospel looks beautiful or is discredited. Where might your daily behaviour be commending or undermining the message you profess?
Grace does not only forgive; it trains us to say no to ungodliness. What is one worldly passion grace is teaching you to renounce right now?
We live between Christ's first appearing and His glorious return. How would living with the blessed hope in view change your priorities this week?
Christ gave Himself to make us a people zealous for good deeds. Does zeal for doing good mark your life, and where is God stirring you toward it?
Older believers here are called to train the younger by example and instruction. Who is pouring godly wisdom into you, and into whom could you be pouring it?

translationNotes.note: Bringing salvation to everyone can be read as grace appearing to all people, offering salvation, rather than teaching that every individual is finally saved; the context speaks of a purified people.
The blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ most naturally, by the Greek construction, calls Jesus both God and Saviour, affirming His deity.
A people for His own possession echoes the Greek term for a treasured possession, recalling Israel in Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 14:2.
